question_text: What are meta-directing groups? Give one example of each.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: A meta-directing group is a group
already present on a benzene ring
which directs the next incoming group
the ring, so they also deactivate it.
steps.why: A group that withdraws electrons lowers the electron density at positions 2 and 4 more than at position 3, so the next substitution takes place at position 3, and it takes place more slowly than on benzene itself. That is why these are also called ring-deactivating groups.
common_mistakes: Giving only the position. The answer also has to say that these groups withdraw electrons and deactivate the ring.
Writing position 4. Para is position 4; meta is position 3.
steps.memory_tip: Meta is position 3, neither neighbouring nor straight across.
steps.margin_note: Write the position number 3 and the words electron withdrawing.

steps.label: The examples
lines: and cyano –CN behave in the same way.
steps.why: Both examples withdraw electrons from the ring, the nitro group through its two oxygen atoms and the carboxy group through its C=O bond, so in both compounds position 3 is where the next substitution takes place.
common_mistakes: Giving –CH₃ as an example. The methyl group releases electrons and directs to positions 2 and 4.
Naming the group without naming a compound that carries it. Write –NO₂ in nitrobenzene.
steps.memory_tip: Electron-withdrawing groups — NO₂, COOH, CHO, SO₃H, CN — direct to meta.
steps.margin_note: One closing line naming the two example groups completes the answer.

insider_note: The position number 3 alone is only half the answer. The other half is that these groups withdraw electrons and deactivate the ring, which is what makes position 3 the site of the next substitution.
